turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have a seat. What's the problem today?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this cough, doctor, every morning without fail, and I'm getting properly puffed just walking. My wife Margaret's been on at me for months, and then a chest infection proper knocked me, so she booked it. I nearly didn't come — the van needed an MOT — but here I am.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's the cough been?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Eight years, easy... no, wait, it started the year I turned fifty, and I'm sixty-two, so twelve years. Every morning there's thick white stuff, I hawk it up over the sink before the kettle's boiled, then I'm all right till the next day. It's been the routine so long I stopped noticing.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood in the phlegm?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never, not a streak. White, like wallpaper paste, except in that infection when it went yellow-green and foul, and that's gone back to white.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Short of breath as well?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Six weeks, that's when I started having to stop — the corner shop's four minutes normally, and now I hold the postbox halfway. Talking does it too, and I do talk, so Margaret gets the pausing. Flat pavement, not even a hill, which is the annoying part.

[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Can I come in on that? It's not six weeks — he's been stopping on that pavement since before Christmas, so three months at least. And he coughs half the night. I'm awake for it; he isn't always aware.

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Margaret, no. I am not coughing the night away — I might clear my throat if I get up for a wee, but I sleep. The stopping-to-breathe thing is six weeks; before that I was just slower, which is being sixty-two and still lugging compost.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wheeze?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Mornings, yes, a little whistle breathing out, till I've had a tea and walked about the kitchen. Not in the daytime, and not when I'm driving the van. Once I'm going it's quiet.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fever at the moment? Swollen ankles?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever now, and my ankles are normal, boots still fit. I was hot and shivery for two days with the infection, proper flu-ey, then it went. I did get the thermometer out — it was up, then it wasn't. Nothing since.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wake up gasping? Weight down?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No gasping in the night. I haven't lost weight either — same hole on the belt. If anything the allotment cake isn't helping, but that's a separate grumble. Trousers fit the way they did in the autumn.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): When was the infection?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I thought a fortnight, but let me get it straight: the amoxicillin finished ten days ago, five hundred milligrams three times a day for five days, from the walk-in GP. I started them the week before they finished. Sputum's been white since the last tablet. I was in bed two days and then back in the van, which was probably stupid.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Breathing worse since than before it?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes — it lifted a bit but never got back to my old self, and that's what worried me, more than the cough I've had for years. I kept thinking another week and it'd settle. It hasn't.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): About ten a day... maybe twenty, if I'm being straight, more when City are on or I'm sat in the van between drops. I tell people ten, and I was on thirty in my thirties. Started at seventeen, so forty-odd years. Mostly Mayfair, with roll-ups at the weekend sometimes.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Inhalers?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The blue one, salbutamol, a hundred micrograms, two puffs when I need them. And the brown, beclometasone, two hundred... no, it's the four hundred microgram inhaler, two puffs twice a day, that's what the label says. I don't do what the label says.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often do you actually take them?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): The brown one, half the days, roughly — if I feel decent I leave it. The blue one lives in my coat for the stairs, and some weeks both just sit there. I know the steroid one is meant to be regular, I read the leaflet. I just don't.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The brown inhaler's been in the kitchen drawer all week. I looked this morning, dust on the cap.

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Not all week, Margaret. I used it yesterday and the day before, both doses those days, I think, just not this morning because we were rushing. So not the full twice a day, but not abandoned in a drawer either. There's a difference.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Other medicines? Any allergies?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine five milligrams, one every morning for four years, for the blood pressure — that's the only tablet. No allergies, and penicillin's fine, I just finished that amoxicillin without a rash or anything. A cousin of mine swelled up with penicillin, but that's her, not me.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Appendix out when I was twenty-two, at the old General. Nothing since — no scopes, no chest drains, nothing like that. I heal all right, if that's any use to you.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Who's at home? Still working?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Margaret and me, bungalow on Mill Lane, thirty years in September. I do three mornings a week in a Transit for Dave Pell, light parcels, nothing heavy now. Weekends I'm on the allotment if the chest allows, and drink-wise it's two pints of bitter on a Saturday and that's the lot.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The van mornings wipe him out, though. He comes in and sits on the kitchen chair a good ten minutes before he'll speak.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): That's me getting my boots off, Margaret. I'm all right after a sit down, it's not dramatic. Tea, five minutes, then I can talk her ear off again, unfortunately for her.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nurse — the numbers.

[SEG0040] person_4 (NURSE): Blood pressure first off was one fifty two over ninety; rechecked just now, one forty six over eighty eight. Pulse ninety two, oxygen saturations ninety three percent on air. Breathing rate twenty two, temperature thirty six point seven.

[SEG0041] person_4 (NURSE): Spirometry, best of three. FEV1 came out one point eight... sorry, one point six eight litres, fifty four percent predicted. FVC three point zero five litres, seventy nine percent predicted, ratio fifty five percent. He coughed on the first blow so we binned that one.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll listen — breathe through your mouth. Wheeze both sides, no crackles. Heart sounds are normal, no swelling at the ankles.

[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Both sides, right. Is fifty four percent dreadful? My dad had emphysema, smoked about forty a day, died at seventy-one, and he was on oxygen near the end. I've been dodging this conversation since the funeral, what with the allotment show and one thing and another.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's low. Smoking history plus these blows — working impression is COPD, not a final label. That infection may still be pulling the numbers down.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): COPD. Do I need oxygen, because of the van and the stairs at Dave's lock-up — I can't be trailing a bottle round the allotment. I'd rather know straight.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. Saturations are ninety three, not oxygen territory. I'll request a chest X-ray, and I'll refer you to the stop-smoking service — they'll go through patches or tablets. No decision today.

[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Patches I could maybe live with. Tablets make me think of my uncle, who went peculiar on a tablet, though that was for his nerves, completely different, I do realise, even while I'm saying it.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Brown inhaler, two puffs twice a day, every day, including the good days. Blue one, two puffs when you're breathless, through a spacer if you can find it.

[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Spacer's in the sideboard, behind the coasters. I'll put the brown one by the kettle so I actually see it, not in that drawer. Mornings I'll remember; evenings I forget if the snooker's on, that's the honest bit. I can do it if it's by the kettle.
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll move it to the kettle tonight. He won't fight me if it's just sitting there.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll move it myself, thank you. I don't need a warden, I need a habit, there's a difference. Sorry, doctor, we're a double act, unfortunately.

[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Back here in six weeks. Sooner if you're breathless just sitting, if you cough blood, or if you're feverish. Bring both inhalers and we'll check your technique. Nurse will book it.
[SEG0053] person_4 (NURSE): I'll book the chest X-ray and the six-week slot, and the stop-smoking referral goes today.

[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks clashes with the parish jumble, but I'll come. Should I bring the boxes as well as the inhalers, because the pharmacist once said my timing was off and I can never remember which way round she meant. She got quite sharp about it.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): The inhalers are enough. We'll sort the timing at that visit.

[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. And the compost — I've been turning a very dry heap, and the morning cough is worse on allotment days, so I did wonder if it's just the dust and not this COPD thing at all. Margaret says I'm clutching at straws.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dust on top, not the cause. Stick to the inhalers. Off you go.
[SEG0058] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll be back in six weeks. Thank you.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Cheers. Sorry for the life story.
